blocks.content: Both instructions move files from the build context into the image. The practical guidance is simple: COPY is the predictable default, ADD is a superset with extra, sometimes surprising, capabilities.
COPY does exactly one thing: it copies files and directories, nothing more. ADD does that too, but adds automatic tar extraction and the ability to fetch content from a remote URL directly.

blocks.alt: COPY does one thing, ADD does that plus extras

blocks.content: 2. Predictability Is the Real Deciding Factor
blocks.text: 2. Predictability Is the Real Deciding Factor

blocks.content: COPY's narrowness is actually its strength: reading COPY src dest, you know exactly what will happen. Reading ADD src dest, you have to know whether src happens to be a tar archive (which changes behavior entirely) or a URL, before you can predict what the instruction actually does.

blocks.alt: Narrower behavior is easier to reason about at a glance

Default to COPY for ordinary file copying, which covers the large majority of Dockerfile needs. Reach for ADD only in the specific case where you genuinely need its extraction or remote-fetch behavior, not as a habit or a shorter-to-type alternative.

blocks.alt: COPY by default, ADD only for its specific extras

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: ADD is a superset of COPY, adding tar auto-extraction and remote URL fetching, capabilities that make its behavior less predictable at a glance.
Default to COPY for ordinary file copying, and reach for ADD deliberately, only when you need what it adds.
